catalog_quote: In a recent study of Balti, (Caplow 2016) found fundamental frequency to be a strong correlate of contrastive stress, suggesting that the transphonologization of stress to tone is a pathway of tonogenesis. While Dzongkha does not have phonological stress, long and short rhymes are analogous to stressed and unstressed syllables (in contrast to Balti for which vowel duration is a weak correlate of stress). Perhaps what is seen here is a manifestation of the transphonologization of length to pitch: a contrast in the duration of the second syllable is manifest on the first syllable in elevated and suppressed pitch distributions, contributing to an emerging melody contrast on the first syllable. ... [p.141] Lexical words are those that take tone, can be uttered in isolation, and are not phonologically bound to any other word. ... Relational words (affixes and enclitics), on the other hand, a…
sweep_summary: Dzongkha (dzon1239, catalog no word stress on Watters 2018 Rice PhD, p.69 'Dzongkha does not have phonological stress'). this search of works with stress in the title has one item, Watters 1996 'A preliminary study of prosody in Dzongkha' (UT Arlington MA thesis, UMI/ProQuest 1383506, already in the per-language bibliography). No open copy exists: ProQuest preview only (saved), Harvard-restricted per the Harvard library catalogue, MPI-EVA CD-ROM per Glottolog, nothing on archive.org, HathiTrust, Google Books; UTA MavMatrix and sil.org record pages unreachable (not reachable by automated download). The author's own 2018 description (pp.6, 23) says the thesis is a segment-and-tone / phonation-pitch acoustic study whose content was folded into Watters 2002 (LTBA 25.1), which is held by the project and was re-read with the p.40 page scan verified: its only stress remarks are impressionistic scare-quoted 'stress' on long first syllables of disyllables in the Dzongkha/Lhomi syllable-tone type, illustrated with Lhomi data, and it concludes the syllable pitches are not phonologically contrastive. Net: the 1996 thesis is judged prosody-but-not-word-stress (unread, medium priority to acquire via ProQuest/ILL for completeness); nothing read this search of works with stress in the title supersedes Watters 2018; Watters 2002 p.40 refines the no-word-stress coding (length-linked prominence, no stress rule). searching was done by automated download/direct download on catalog APIs and known repositories only.

new_statements.quote: I now turn to a discussion of pitch when it is in the domain of the syllable, as in Dzongkha and Lhomi. The pitch pattern in disyllabic nouns for these two languages is considerably more complex than in monosyllabic words. I illustrate this discussion, again, with data from Lhomi. Vowel length is contrastive on the first syllable of disyllabic words, but not on the second syllable. When the first syllable is long it attracts stress, or perhaps it is because this syllable is stressed that it is lengthened. In any case, this syllable is "heavy" in comparison to the one which follows it. When the first syllable is short, the first and second syllables seem to be of equal "weight" in terms of quantity and "stress."

new_statements.reading: For the syllable-tone type that Watters assigns to Dzongkha and Lhomi, he reports an impressionistic, scare-quoted 'stress' on a long first syllable of disyllables (long CVV.CV = heavy-light, short CV.CV = equal weight), with pitch (level/rising vs falling) derived from onset phonation and rhyme weight; the illustration is Lhomi data, not Dzongkha, and p.44 concludes the syllable pitches 'are not phonologically contrastive'. This refines the catalog's no word stress record (length-linked prominence, no fixed stress rule) but does not contradict it; the same author's 2018 grammar, the catalog's deciding source, states explicitly that Dzongkha has no phonological stress and treats long/short rhymes as merely analogous to stressed/unstressed syllables. Already logged as 'refines' in by the 2026-09-16 access pass.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both fragments of the deciding quotation are verbatim in the Watters 2018 PDF we hold at the stated places (printed p.69 = p.90, ch.3 intro; printed p.141 = p.162). (2) Deciding source: a 2018 642-pp dissertation reference grammar with an acoustic prosody chapter, by the field's main worker on Dzongkha prosody; the denial of phonological stress is explicit ('While Dzongkha does not have phonological stress..'), and the grammar's word-class criteria are tonal (lexical words 'take tone'; bound relational morphemes 'do not take stress' and fall under the host's tone). (3) Cross-checks downloaded now: Tshering & van Driem 2019 (709 pp, open access) describes only register tone, contour tone and vowel length and never mentions word stress (consistent/silent); Watters 2002 LTBA speaks of a long first syllable 'attracting stress' in scare quotes for the Dzongkha/Lhomi type
